item.title: The Plant – Martin Kaloshi: On Resonance

item.description: See, before this class, I held the common conviction that electrons lie on atoms. They might shift from one atom to another, or even from one compound (multiple atoms together) to another, but at any stable moment in time, electrons are positioned on a single atom of their choice.

item.title: The Plant: The Existential Horror of AI
item.dc:creator: The Plant
item.description: October— while being a time of laughter, candy and silly costumes— can also be a time that makes us reflect on our fears. A fear is never just a fear, it’s always rooted in something deeper. The older I grow, the less afraid I am of the things that go bump in the night. The supernatural creatures of the world don’t keep me up anymore, the world we live in does.

item.title: The Plant – Karina Awad-Battista: Come for the Borsch. Stay for the Culture.
item.dc:creator: Karina Awad-Battista
item.description: For those of you who are unaware, borsch is a traditional soup dish originating from Ukraine. There are infinite variations, but the most well-known is made with beets and garnished with sour cream, served with some bread rolls on the side. Today, borsch is a staple in many Eastern European households and is seen as an integral part of Ukrainian culture.

item.title: The Plant – Leo Baron: The Iceberg of Safdie’s Stairs
item.dc:creator: Leo Baron
item.description: It’s a funny thing. Online, the Safdie stairs have been seriously condemned for their hazardous nature. This is true. The stairs have the potential to make an inattentive person fall. Does a piece of art need to ask for the user’s consent beforehand? According to the Régie du batiment du Quebec (RBQ), implemented a decade after the stairs’ installment, by law, Safdie’s creation shouldn’t exist.

item.title: The McGill Daily: Keeping our unhoused community warm this winter
item.dc:creator: The McGill Daily
item.description: Investing in warming shelters is not enough, as shelters and homes are not synonymous. This distinction is especially pertinent for “situational” or “hidden homelessness,” where people seek shelter in their vehicles, hotels, and other forms of temporary housing. Nonetheless, some individuals find themselves in the visible category of being unhoused, falling under cyclical or chronic subtypes.
